results.statement_tex:
\begin{definition}
An operator is \emph{nondecreasing} if
\[
 \forall (x,u),(y,v)\in\gra f:\qquad (x-y)(u-v)\geq0,
\]
and \emph{nonincreasing} if $-f$ is nondecreasing. It is \emph{maximally monotone} in a specified orientation if its graph has no proper monotone extension of that orientation.
For a nondecreasing monotone operator, this is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:maximality}
 \forall(x,u)\in\R^2,\quad
 \left[\forall(y,v)\in\gra f,\ (x-y)(u-v)\ge0\right]
 \Longrightarrow (x,u)\in\gra f.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, in contrapositive form,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:maximalitycontra}
 \forall(x,u)\notin\gra f,\quad
 \exists(y,v)\in\gra f:\ (x-y)(u-v)<0.
\end{equation}
For the nonincreasing orientation, replace $\ge0$ by $\le0$ in
\eqref{eq:maximality} and $<0$ by $>0$ in \eqref{eq:maximalitycontra}.
Denote these two classes by $\Mu$ and $\Md$.
\end{definition}

results.statement_tex:
\begin{definition}[Maximal completion and completed restriction]\label{def:completedrestriction}
Let $I=(a,b)\ne\varnothing$ and let $h:I\to\R$ be nondecreasing.
Write $h(x\pm)$ for its one-sided limits, in the extended real line.
Its \emph{maximal completion} $\widehat h$ is
\[
 \widehat h(x)=
 \begin{cases}
  [h(x-),h(x+)],&a<x<b,\\
  (-\infty,h(a+)]\cap\R,&x=a\in\R,\\
  [h(b-),+\infty)\cap\R,&x=b\in\R,\\
  \varnothing,&x\notin\overline I.
 \end{cases}
\]
For nonincreasing $h$, set $\widehat h:=-\widehat{(-h)}$.

For $f\in\Mu\cup\Md$ and a nonempty open interval
$I\subseteq\operatorname{int}\dom f$, the \emph{completed restriction}
$f|_I$ is the unique maximally monotone operator of the same orientation
satisfying
\[
 \forall x\in I:\qquad (f|_I)(x)=f(x),\qquad
 \dom(f|_I)\subseteq\overline I.
\]
\end{definition}

results.statement_tex:
\begin{example}[Survival and tail quantile operators]\label{ex:survival}
For a real random variable $X$, the survival function
$t\mapsto\PP(X>t)$ is nonincreasing. Its left and right limits
at $t$ are $\PP(X\geq t)$ and $\PP(X>t)$.
The operator $\SSS[X]$ fills each jump with the interval between
these limits, so it is maximally nonincreasing by
Definition~\ref{def:completedrestriction}.
Its inverse $\TT[X]$ is also maximally nonincreasing, since
inversion preserves maximality and orientation.

For $0<p<1$, $\TT[X](p)$ is a nonempty bounded closed interval.
If $q$ is a measurable selection of $\TT[X]$ and $U$ is uniform
on $(0,1)$, then $q(U)$ has the law of $X$: the set
$\{p\in(0,1):q(p)>t\}$ has length $\PP(X>t)$.
\end{example}

results.statement_tex:
\begin{proposition}[Nonnegative products]\label{prop:products}
Let $f,g$ be maximal with the same orientation. If
\[
 \ran f\cup\ran g\subset[0,\infty),
\]
then $fg$ is monotone with that orientation, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:productcriterion}
 fg\text{ is maximal}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \dom f\cap\dom g=\R
 \ \text{or}\ \ran(fg)\ne\{0\}.
\end{equation}
When maximal,
\[
 \ran(fg)=\ran f\,\ran g.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Lattice median]\label{prop:latticemedian}
Let $r\ge0$ be an integer, set $n=2r+1$ and
$[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ be
maximal operators of the same orientation. The two finite lattice
expressions
\begin{equation}\label{eq:median}
 m:=\operatorname{med}(f_1,\ldots,f_n)
  =\inf_{\substack{J\subseteq[n]\\|J|=r+1}}\sup_{i\in J}f_i
  =\sup_{\substack{J\subseteq[n]\\|J|=r+1}}\inf_{i\in J}f_i
\end{equation}
coincide and define the \emph{operator median}, a maximal operator
satisfying, simultaneously for every $z\in\R$ and $\lambda>0$,
\[
 J_{\lambda m}(z)=\operatorname{med}_{1\le i\le n}J_{\lambda f_i}(z).
\]
If at least $r+1$ of the $f_i$ lie between maximal operators $\ell$ and $h$ of that orientation, then $\ell\le m\le h$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{example}[Multilevel concentration for a product]
\label{ex:productmultilevel}
Let $n\geq1$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be real random variables.
Let $a_i\in\R\setminus \{0\}$, $\sigma_i>0$,
and $\alpha\in\Md$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positiveprofile}
 \begin{aligned}
 &\dom\alpha=[0,\infty),\\
 &\forall t>0:\qquad \alpha(t)\subset[0,1],\\
 &\forall i\in[n]:\qquad
   \SSS[|X_i-a_i|]\leq\alpha\circ\frac{\id}{\sigma_i}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
We bound the deviation $Y:=|\prod_{i=1}^nX_i-\prod_{i=1}^na_i|$.
For every $r\geq0$, expanding the product shows that $Y\leq P(r)$
whenever, for every $i\in[n]$, $|X_i-a_i|\leq\sigma_i r$, where
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 P(r)&:=\prod_{i=1}^n(|a_i|+\sigma_i r)-\prod_{i=1}^n|a_i|
       =\sum_{k=1}^n c_k r^k,\\
 c_k&:=\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\\|A|=k}}
            \prod_{i\in A}\sigma_i\prod_{i\notin A}|a_i|.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Since $c_n=\prod_i\sigma_i>0$, $P$ is an increasing bijection of
$[0,\infty)$. The union bound therefore gives
$\SSS[Y]\leq n(\alpha\circ P^{-1})$.

We now rewrite this bound using the parallel-sum calculus.
All inverse powers below are ordinary maps on $[0,\infty)$;
their composites with $\alpha$ include the completed value at zero.
Since $P$ is the sum of its monomials,
\[
 P^{-1}=\mathop{\boxplus}_{k\in [n]}
                 \left(\frac{\id}{c_k}\right)^{1/k}.
\]
For these maps, left composition by $\alpha$ distributes over the
parallel sum. Proposition~\ref{prop:envelopes} then gives, for
$\theta_k>0$ with $\sum_{k\in [n]}\theta_k=1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:productmultilevelprofile}
 \begin{aligned}
 \SSS[Y]
 &\leq n(\alpha\circ P^{-1})
   =n\left(\mathop{\boxplus}_{k\in [n]}
       \left[\alpha\circ
         \left(\frac{\id}{c_k}\right)^{1/k}\right]\right)\\
 &\leq n\sup_{k\in [n]}
       \left(\alpha\circ
           \left(\frac{\theta_k\id}{c_k}\right)^{1/k}\right).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The distributive identity also holds at jumps: if
$I=\alpha^{-1}(u)$ is a nonempty interval, the inverses of both
sides take the same value $P(I)=\sum_{k\in [n]}c_k I^k$ at $u$.

For example, for $t>0$ set $\alpha(t)=e^{-t^2}$ and take its maximal
completion. If $d$ is the number of positive coefficients $c_k$, choosing

results.statement_tex:
\begin{definition}[Scalar integration]\label{def:area}
Let $f\in\Mu\cup\Md$ have nonempty domain interior $I$.
For $a<b$ with $(a,b)\subseteq I$, choose a measurable selection
$s$ of $f$ on $(a,b)$ and write
\[
 \int_a^b f(t)\,dt:=\int_a^b s(t)\,dt,
 \qquad
 \int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt:=\int_a^b |s(t)|\,dt.
\]
We allow infinite endpoints and extended scalar integrals whenever
the positive and negative parts are not both infinite.
We call $f$ integrable on $(a,b)$ if $\int_a^b|f(t)|\,dt<\infty$.
Adding or removing endpoints does not change these integrals.
For reversed limits, set $\int_b^a f=-\int_a^b f$, and set
$\int_a^a f=0$. Other Borel scalar expressions in $f$ are integrated
through the same selection convention whenever their integrals exist.

We call $f$ \emph{integrable} if it is integrable on its domain
interior $I$, that is, if $\int_I|f(t)|\,dt<\infty$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Aumann integration of a monotone family]
\label{thm:familyintegral}
The integral in Definition~\ref{def:familyintegral} is well defined,
with values on $I$ given by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:integralvalues}

integration preserves the pointwise resolvent order, is additive,

\begin{proposition}[Order and algebraic properties of the Hardy transform]\label{prop:hardycalculus}
Let $f,g\in\Md$ be integrable, with common domain interior
$I=(0,L)$ for some $L\in(0,\infty]$. Then, for every $\lambda>0$,
\[
 \mathcal H(f+g)=\mathcal H(f)+\mathcal H(g),\qquad \mathcal H(\lambda f)=\lambda \mathcal H(f).
\]
Moreover, $f\leq \mathcal H(f)$, and $f\leq g$ implies $\mathcal H(f)\leq \mathcal H(g)$.
The latter assertion also holds for integrable $f,g\in\Md$ with
respective domain interiors $(0,L_f)$ and $(0,L_g)$,
where $L_f,L_g\in(0,\infty]$.
\end{proposition}

results.statement_tex:
\begin{example}[Superadditive transformation of an $\ell^q$-norm]
\label{ex:normtransform}
Let $n\ge1$ and $1\le q\le\infty$. For $x\in[0,\infty)^n$, set
$F(x):=\|x\|_q$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normtransform}
 \forall a\in[0,\infty)^n:\qquad
 F^\sharp(a)=\|a\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i.
\end{equation}
For every admissible family in \eqref{eq:superadditivetransform},
\[
 \sum_j\|v^{(j)}\|_q
 \le\sum_j\|v^{(j)}\|_1
 =\left\|\sum_jv^{(j)}\right\|_1
 \le\|a\|_1.
\]
Conversely, the family $v^{(i)}=a_i e_i$, where $e_i$ is the $i$th
coordinate vector, is admissible and satisfies
$\sum_i\|a_i e_i\|_q=\sum_i a_i$. This proves
\eqref{eq:normtransform}. For example, for the Euclidean norm,
$F(\mathbbm{1})=\sqrt n$ while $F^\sharp(\mathbbm{1})=n$.

Consequently, Proposition~\ref{prop:hardytailaggregation} below gives,
for nonnegative integrable random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ and
$0<p<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hardytailnorm}
 \mathcal H\left(\TT[\|(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\|_q]\right)
 \le\sum_{i=1}^n\mathcal H(\TT[X_i]).
\end{equation}
Theorem~\ref{thm:hardytailaggregationsharp} shows that this bound is
sharp, even for finite-valued comonotone variables.
Thus, when only the individual upper-tail averages are prescribed,
the best bound for the upper-tail average of the norm is their sum,
for every $q\in[1,\infty]$. The extremizing construction uses large
coordinate values at successively rarer probability scales.

For $0<q\le1$, the function
$F(x):=\|x\|_q=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^q)^{1/q}$ (a quasi-norm for $q<1$)
is superadditive on $[0,\infty)^n$, so
$F^\sharp(a)=F(a)=\|a\|_q$.
\end{example}

results.statement_tex:
\begin{example}[Heterogeneous estimators: median and normalized sum]
\label{ex:heterogeneousestimators}
Let $\widehat\theta_1,\widehat\theta_2,\widehat\theta_3$ be integrable
scalar estimators of $\theta\in\R$. Set
\[
 \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{med}}
 :=\operatorname{med}(\widehat\theta_1,\widehat\theta_2,\widehat\theta_3),
 \qquad
 \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{av}}:=\frac13\sum_{i=1}^3\widehat\theta_i.
\]
Fix $p\in(0,1)$ and write
\[
 \forall i\in[3]:\qquad
 a_i:=\mathcal H\bigl(\TT[|\widehat\theta_i-\theta|]\bigr)(p).
\]
Let $a_{(1)}\leq a_{(2)}\leq a_{(3)}$ be these upper-tail means
in increasing order. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:heterogeneousestimators}
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal H\bigl(\TT[|\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{med}}-\theta|]\bigr)(p)
 &\leq\min\left\{a_{(1)}+a_{(2)},\frac{a_1+a_2+a_3}{2}\right\},\\
 \mathcal H\bigl(\TT[|\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{av}}-\theta|]\bigr)(p)
 &\leq\frac{a_1+a_2+a_3}{3}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For the first bound, apply Corollary~\ref{cor:hardymedian} to the
absolute errors and use
\[
 |\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{med}}-\theta|
 \leq\operatorname{med}(|\widehat\theta_1-\theta|,
                       |\widehat\theta_2-\theta|,
                       |\widehat\theta_3-\theta|).
\]
The second bound follows from the triangle inequality and
Proposition~\ref{prop:hardytailaggregation} with
$F(x)=(x_1+x_2+x_3)/3$.
The median bound can omit the largest upper-tail mean, whereas the
bound for the normalized sum includes all three.

For a concrete illustration, let $Z\geq0$ satisfy $0<\E Z<\infty$
and let $b>6$. Take
\[
 \widehat\theta_1=\theta+Z,\qquad
 \widehat\theta_2=\theta+2Z,\qquad
 \widehat\theta_3=\theta+bZ.
\]
Writing $h:=\mathcal H(\TT[Z])(p)$, the marginal upper-tail means
are $(h,2h,bh)$. The bounds in \eqref{eq:heterogeneousestimators}
are therefore $3h$ for the median and $(b+3)h/3$ for the normalized
sum. The latter is larger and grows with $b$.
This difference can also be seen in the actual errors, since
\[
 \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{med}}-\theta=2Z,\qquad
 \widehat\theta_{\mathrm{av}}-\theta=\frac{b+3}{3}Z.
\]
Thus a single estimator with an arbitrarily large error scale can
spoil the normalized sum while the median remains controlled.
Permuting the inputs leaves both formulas unchanged, so this
comparison does not require knowing the index of the poor estimator.
\end{example}

results.statement_tex:
\begin{definition}[Geometric Hardy transform]
\label{def:geometrichardytransform}
Let $q\in\Md$ have domain interior $I=(0,1)$ and nonnegative
values on $I$, with
\[
 \int_0^1\log_+q(s)\,ds<\infty.
\]
If $q$ does not vanish identically on $I$, its
\emph{geometric Hardy transform} $\mathcal G(q)$ is the unique
maximally nonincreasing extension of
\[
 \exp\circ\mathcal H\bigl(\log\circ\sup\{q,0\}\bigr)
\]
having domain interior $I$ and nonnegative values on $I$.
If $q$ vanishes identically on $I$, set $\mathcal G(q)=q$.

Equivalently, $\mathcal G(q)$ is the maximal decreasing completion
on $\overline I$ of the classical \emph{geometric mean operator}
defined on $(0,1)$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-geometric-definition}
 u\longmapsto
 \exp\left(\frac1u\int_0^u\log q(s)\,ds\right),
\end{equation}
with $\log0=-\infty$ and $\exp(-\infty)=0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}[A zero-induced jump of the geometric average]
\label{ex:local-geometric-zero-jump}
Let $q$ be the maximal completion on $I$ of the continuous profile
\[
 \forall u\in(0,1):\qquad q(u)=\max\{1-2u,0\}.
\]
Although $q(1/2)=0$, the logarithm is integrable up to this level:
\[
 \int_0^{1/2}\log(1-2s)\,ds=-\frac12.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \lim_{u\uparrow1/2}\mathcal G(q)(u)
 =\exp\left(2\int_0^{1/2}\log(1-2s)\,ds\right)
 =\mathrm e^{-1}.
\]
For every $u>1/2$, however, $q$ vanishes on the interval $(1/2,u)$,
so $\int_0^u\log q=-\infty$ and $\mathcal G(q)(u)=0$.
Maximal completion therefore fills the jump by setting
\[
 \mathcal G(q)(1/2)=[0,\mathrm e^{-1}].
\]
Here $\log q$ is finite on $(0,1/2)$, and $1/2$ is the upper
endpoint of the domain of its Hardy transform. The jump of
$\mathcal G(q)$ occurs at this boundary, which lies inside $I$.
Figure~\ref{fig:geometric-zero-jump} compares $q$, $\mathcal G(q)$
and the continuous Hardy average $\mathcal H(q)$.
\end{example}

results.statement_tex:
\begin{example}[Subgaussian concentration and depth]
Suppose $q_\Delta(u)\leq A\sqrt{\log(2/u)}$ and
$p_0=\cdots=p_L=d$. Set $R(u)=\sqrt{\log(24\mathrm e/u)}$.
By \eqref{eq:hardy-geometric-comparison} and Jensen's inequality,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-network-depth}
 \PP\!\left(
 \begin{aligned}
 |V-m_V|&>
 A\sqrt{\frac{1+NL/2}{d}}\,R(u)
 \\
 &\quad{}\times\left(
 \max\{m_x,m_1,\ldots,m_L\}
 +\frac{AR(u)}{\sqrt{d\min\{N,2\}}}
 \right)^L
 \end{aligned}
 \right)\leq u.
\end{equation}
The confidence constants do not grow with $L$, but the complete
bound does. Independent standard Gaussian entries allow $A=2$ and
medians satisfying $m_x\leq1+\sqrt{2\log2/(Nd)}$ and
$m_\ell\leq\sqrt2+\sqrt{\log2/d}$
\cite[Theorem~5.32 and Proposition~5.34]{Vershynin2012Introduction}.

For fixed $L$, $N\asymp d$, and uniformly bounded $A,m_x,m_\ell$,
\eqref{eq:local-network-depth} gives, up to constants depending on
these bounds and on $L$, the tail rate
$\min\{t^2,d^{L/(L+1)}t^{2/(L+1)}\}$ of Adamczak
\cite[Theorem~3.7]{Adamczak2025NonlinearMatrices}.
In this subgaussian setting, the concentration behavior is
essentially the same as in Adamczak's result; his work covers many
more settings, including batch estimates
\cite[Theorem~3.14]{Adamczak2025NonlinearMatrices}.
\end{example}

results.statement_tex:
\begin{lemma}[Power--geometric limit]\label{lem:powergeometric}
For $a,b>0$, $\kappa>0$ and $0\leq\lambda\leq1$, set
\[
 m_{\kappa,\lambda}(a,b)
 =\bigl(\lambda a^{-1/\kappa}+(1-\lambda)b^{-1/\kappa}\bigr)^{-\kappa}.
\]
Then $m_{\kappa,\lambda}(a,b)\to a^\lambda b^{1-\lambda}$ as $\kappa\to\infty$.
\end{lemma}
